name: Receiving Input Integers Until a Certain Condition is Met (Case 1)
description: Construct a program that receives an integer from the user, outputs that integer, and stops receiving integers when the user enters a negative integer.
code:
#Step 1: Read the first integer that the user enters
text = input("Enter an integer:")
num = int(text)
#Step 2: Print the integer that the user has entered, then receive the next integers as long as the user enters an integer that is not negative;; otherwise stop
while num >= 0 :
    print("The integer entered is:", num)
    text = input("Enter an integer:")
    num = int(text)
print("End of input.")

1.content: #Step 1: Read the first integer that the user enters

commentList: Purpose: this line shows the prompt "Enter an integer:" to the user, waits for the user to type something and press Enter, and saves whatever the user typed in the variable text so you can use it later.

Syntax breakdown: on the left you have the variable name text, = is the assignment operator, and on the right you call the input(...) function with a string literal prompt. The result returned by input(...) is assigned to text.
Semantics: input(...) pauses the program until you provide input. The value stored in text is always a string (for example, typing 5 stores the string "5").

Common errors and misconceptions: you might expect input to give a number, but it gives text. If you later call int(text) and the user typed something that is not a valid integer (like "abc" or an empty line), that conversion will fail and cause an error. Also be aware that unusual console actions (EOF) can make input raise an error in some environments.

Best practices: make the prompt clear (for example include "(negative to stop)"), trim whitespace with text = text.strip() if you need, and validate or convert the string using try/except around int(text) so you can handle non-integer input gracefully instead of crashing.

Improvement tip: you can prevent problems by looping until you get a valid integer from the user (or explicitly handle the case where the user types invalid text) before continuing with the rest of the program.

Purpose: This line converts the string you got from input() into an integer and saves that number in the variable num so you can do numeric checks and arithmetic later (for example, the while condition).
Syntax & semantics: num is a variable name, = is the assignment operator, and int(text) calls Python's int() function to parse the contents of the string text into an integer value.
What can go wrong: If the user typed something that is not a valid integer text (for example 'abc' or '3.5'), int(text) will raise a ValueError and your program will crash unless you handle it.

Common misconception: You might think int() will convert any numeric-looking string (like '3.5') by rounding or truncating, but int('3.5') is invalid and raises an error. Only properly formatted integer strings like '3' or '-2' work. (Note: int(3.5) as a number would truncate, but int('3.5') is not allowed.)

Best practices: You should validate or handle bad input before converting — for example, use text = text.strip() to remove extra spaces and wrap int(text) in a try/except block to catch ValueError and re-prompt the user if needed.

4.content: #Step 2: Print the integer that the user has entered, then receive the next integers as long as the user enters an integer that is not negative;; otherwise stop

commentList: Purpose: You start a loop here that keeps the program printing and reading integers as long as the current value in num is non-negative (zero or positive); this line controls when the program stops accepting more numbers.

Syntax and structure: 'while' is the loop keyword, 'num >= 0' is the condition being tested, and the trailing ':' tells Python that the indented lines that follow belong to the loop body; you must keep the following lines indented.

How it runs (semantics): You should know this is a pre-test loop — Python checks the condition before each iteration. If num is negative at the check, the loop body is skipped and execution continues after the loop.

Common errors and misconceptions: If you forget the ':' or use '=' instead of a comparison operator, Python will raise a syntax error. If num is a string (because you didn't convert input to int), the comparison will raise a TypeError. If you never update num inside the loop, you'll create an infinite loop.

Best practices: Make sure you have converted and validated num as an integer before this line, include the input-and-convert steps inside the loop so num can change each iteration, and keep the condition simple and clear (num >= 0) so the stop condition is easy to understand.
Purpose: You print the current value of num so the program shows the integer the user entered before asking for the next one.

Syntax and meaning: print('The integer entered is:', num) calls the print function with two arguments — a string and the variable num. Python converts num to text for output and places a space between the arguments by default.
Output behavior: print adds a newline after each call, so each printed integer appears on its own line in the program output.
Loop relation: This line is inside the while num >= 0 loop, so you only execute this print when num is non-negative. If the user enters a negative number first, you never reach this line.

Common mistakes: If you write 'The integer entered is: ' + num you will get a TypeError because you cannot concatenate a string and an int. Fix this by using a comma (as shown), str(num), or an f-string.
Best practice: Use clear formatting for readability, for example print(f'The integer entered is: {num}'), which avoids accidental spacing or type-conversion errors and keeps the output tidy.
Purpose: this line asks the user for the next integer (as text) every time the loop repeats so the loop can make progress and eventually stop when a negative number is entered.
Syntax and meaning: input("Enter an integer:") shows the prompt and returns the user's response as a string; that string is stored in the variable text for the next step to convert to an integer.

Common mistakes and errors: input() by itself does not convert the value to an int—if you forget the following int(text) (Line 8) or move this input outside the while block, the loop will never see a new number and can become an infinite loop. Also, if the user types non-numeric text, int(text) will raise a ValueError.

Best practices: you can combine reading and conversion in one line (for example num = int(input(...))) to reduce variables, or better, wrap the conversion in a try/except so you handle non-integer input gracefully. Keep this line indented inside the loop so you read a new value on each iteration.
Purpose: This line converts the most recent user input stored in text into an integer and assigns that value to num so the loop can check the updated number and decide whether to continue or stop.

Syntax and semantics: int(text) calls Python's built-in function to parse the string text into an integer; the = operator stores that integer in the variable num. Because this line is indented inside the while loop, you run it on each iteration to update num.

Potential errors and misconceptions: If the user types something that is not a valid integer string (for example 'abc', '3.5', or an empty string), int(text) will raise a ValueError. Also note that negative numbers convert fine — they simply make the loop condition num >= 0 false and cause the loop to exit. If you omit this assignment, num never changes and the loop can become infinite.

Best practices: Validate or handle conversion errors by using try/except around int(text) or by cleaning the input (for example text = text.strip()) before converting. Provide clear prompts and error messages so the user knows to enter an integer.
You use Line 9 (print("End of input.")) to show the user a final message that the program has stopped receiving integers; it signals the end of the interaction.
You placed this line outside the while loop (no indentation), so you execute it exactly once after the loop finishes — the loop finishes when the user enters a negative integer.
You are calling Python's built-in print function with a string literal as its argument: print(...) writes the text to the console and adds a newline by default; the text is written between quotes.

Be careful: if you accidentally indent this line so it's inside the while loop, you will print the message repeatedly on every iteration. Also, in Python 3 you must keep the parentheses — omitting them or using mismatched quotes will cause a syntax error.

Don't expect this line to print the negative number that stopped the input — you only print numbers inside the loop before reading the negative value. If you want to show that last value, explicitly include it, for example: print('End of input. Last entered:', num).
As a best practice, keep the final message clear and concise, place it outside the loop so it appears once, and use consistent quoting and spacing so your code is easy for you and others to read.

You might pick this because you think the program should only keep reading when the user enters positive numbers, so you use '>' instead of allowing zero. If you use this line, the loop will stop not only for negative inputs but also when the user enters 0. That means entering 0 will end input even though the specification expects the program to continue for non-negative values. In practice, your program will print positive numbers correctly, but it will stop prematurely when the user types 0. The error comes from the boundary test around zero — the condition excludes zero when the intended behavior is to include it.

commentList: You might choose this because many exercises use 0 as a sentinel, so you assume the loop should continue while the value is not zero. If you use this line, the loop will continue for negative numbers (because a negative number is not equal to zero) and will only stop when the user enters 0. That directly contradicts the requirement to stop when the user enters a negative integer. With this condition the program will accept and print negative integers instead of stopping on them, and will only terminate when 0 is entered.

The mistake is a misuse of the logical 'and' — it creates a stricter condition than intended and excludes a valid case (zero).
